content.markdown:
# Joint project: a tested post-quantum migration path for KL-HSM

## Verified facts
- Kriptolog describes constrained KL-HSM flash and RAM, ruling out an assumed drop-in replacement. Its cryptographic firmware uses C on ARM Cortex-M; feasibility therefore concerns the actual product configuration. [F1]
- The company has not adapted its architecture for larger keys or different signature flows. It wants a roadmap identifying supporting firmware versions, performance trade-offs and hybrid classical/post-quantum transition behaviour. [F2]
- Kriptolog seeks a documented roadmap and at least one working integration proof of concept inside twelve months. Its collaborative engineering capacity is modest and depends on a well-defined, practically applicable scope. [F3]
- The company lists PKCS#11 integration and a Common Criteria EAL4+ target. Architecture changes need assessment against these interfaces and evaluation requirements; a research prototype is not certification. [F4]
- Nikolić prefers real-hardware collaboration with measurable deliverables. If an SLE97 route is explored, her laboratory has only two evaluation kits; her notes identify additional partner hardware as helpful. [F5]
- Nikolić’s work implements Dilithium and Falcon signatures in C. Her separate Dilithium study reports compiler-dependent timing leakage, making optimisation-related leakage a concrete risk rather than assuming constant-time source code suffices. [F6]
- Her published hybrid HSM uses classical ECDH and FPGA-assisted Kyber key encapsulation. That evidence concerns key exchange, not hybrid firmware signing. [F7]

## Potential benefits
- For the company: The experiment could establish whether a firmware-based migration is feasible on the selected KL-HSM and provide measured evidence for client-facing version and transition decisions.
- For the researcher: Subject to agreement and access, Nikolić could test how standardised ML-DSA and hybrid signing behave under real HSM memory, toolchain and interoperability constraints.

## Our inference
- This suggests a practical joint project combining target-specific benchmarking with migration design. Finalist-era Dilithium measurements do not validate standardised ML-DSA on KL-HSM, and hybrid key-exchange results do not establish hybrid signing; both transfers need direct testing.
- Joint-project participation is open, but Nikolić’s current availability is unknown. This proposal is conditional on confirming her capacity and agreeing company staffing, hardware access and scope.

## Proposed next steps
- Propose a six-week first experiment on one agreed KL-HSM configuration using production tooling and non-production keys. Kriptolog would supply hardware, firmware support and representative signing workloads; Nikolić would lead porting and measurement. Compare existing RSA/ECDSA signing, standardised ML-DSA and end-to-end hybrid signing/verification. Use known-answer tests and separate tuning/evaluation message sets, checking their independence. Measure correctness, peak RAM, flash, signing latency, throughput, signature/key storage, verifier compatibility and timing leakage. Before testing, negotiate numerical resource/performance limits and a leakage-screening protocol. Go/no-go should assess the best tested configuration against those limits, zero correctness failures, agreed hybrid acceptance/downgrade tests, PKCS#11 compatibility and certification-impact review—not require one method to beat another. Continuation should also require a credible, staffed path to a working integration and an approved versioned roadmap within twelve months, covering larger keys, changed flows and measured trade-offs.
- If the initial gate passes, propose staged integration and regression testing through the twelve-month window. Draft the roadmap alongside implementation, distinguishing experimental support, production-readiness work and certification milestones. Recheck timing and memory after toolchain changes; plan separate side-channel and fault-injection work because initial timing screening cannot establish complete implementation security.

## Open questions
- Can Nikolić confirm availability, a start date and time allocation for this joint project, and can Kriptolog confirm engineering support and budget?
- Which KL-HSM configuration, signing use case, ML-DSA parameters and client verifiers should be covered, and what numerical memory, latency and throughput limits must apply?
- Can Kriptolog provide representative hardware, source/build access, prototype code and a safe non-production-key setup under agreed confidentiality and intellectual-property terms?
- What hybrid acceptance, downgrade-prevention and key-lifecycle rules are required, what is the current Common Criteria status, and who will approve security acceptance criteria and the versioned roadmap?
